The town clock was seven minutes slow, which suited almost everyone.

The baker said it gave his bread a better chance. Schoolchildren preferred it because the first bell seemed to arrive reluctantly. Even the mayor, who had promised to fix it during three separate campaigns, admitted privately that the clock made him feel younger.

Only Mara objected.

She repaired watches in a shop beneath the clock tower, and every morning at eight she heard the great bell sound seven minutes after her own precise little clocks had chimed. She had written letters. She had offered her services for free. She had once climbed halfway up the tower with a toolbox before the caretaker found her and threatened to call the police.

Then one winter the caretaker died, and the mayor gave Mara the key.

The mechanism was older than she expected. Its iron teeth were worn smooth, its weights patched with lead. There was a nest behind the western dial containing three blue buttons and the bones of something small.

She found the problem quickly: a bent arm, easily straightened. But beside it lay a folded piece of paper, yellow and brittle. In an unsteady hand someone had written:

*Please leave it. He said he would be home at six.*

There was no name.

Mara sat on the dusty floor with the note in her lap. Outside, people crossed the square with their collars turned up. A delivery van stopped at the baker’s. A boy dropped a mitten, and a woman ran after him carrying it.

At six, the bell rang seven minutes late.

Mara folded the note and put it in her pocket. Then she straightened the arm.

The next morning, people were annoyed. Several missed the bus because they had come to trust the old clock’s lateness. The baker burned a tray of rolls, though he blamed the flour. The mayor took credit in a short speech that nobody attended.

Mara returned to her shop and opened the door. On the counter she placed a small glass dish containing three blue buttons. Customers sometimes asked where they had come from.

“The tower,” she said.

“Why were they there?”

“I don’t know.”

And when they asked about the clock, she told them it had been an easy repair.
